clue.text: Rolling Stone review initially delighted musician

indicators.note: something rolling tumbles over and over, so the letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the next word counts

parts.note: first letter of delighted

explanation.surface: A Rolling Stone magazine review leaves a performer pleased.
explanation.walkthrough: Rolling Stone looks like the magazine's name, italicised in print, but 'Rolling' is the anagram signal working on 'Stone review' plus D.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevie Wonder is a famous American singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist, so he is an example of a musician.

clue.text: The terms of this fresh scheme absolutely matter!

indicators.note: a term can be an end or limit, so the terms of words are their final letters

parts.note: the final letters of this, fresh and scheme
bang means absolutely or exactly, as in bang on or bang up to date

explanation.surface: A warning that the small print of a new plan really is important.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matter' looks like a verb finishing the sentence, but it is the noun definition. 'Terms' here means ends, not contract conditions.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebang is an affair or business, best known from the idiom 'the whole shebang', meaning the entire thing.

clue.text: Feeling of ecstasy comes with travelling

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
travelling is being in motion

explanation.surface: The feeling of ecstasy that comes from going on a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feeling of ecstasy' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'Feeling' and ecstasy is the drug, abbreviated to E.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotion is a feeling such as joy, anger or sadness, so the two are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Digger finally departs from highway, leaving nothing behind

indicators.note: whatever departs leaves, so that letter is taken out of the longer word

parts.note: an interstate is a US highway

indicators.note: finally points to the very end, so only the closing letter of the word is used

parts.note: last letter of Digger

explanation.surface: A mechanical digger pulls off a motorway, leaving no mess behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove R from INTERSTATE, an American highway. 'Leaving nothing behind' sounds like a tidy departure but means leaving no will.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who dies intestate dies without a valid will, so in legal terms they leave no instructions for their estate.

clue.text: Garments in wide, upright box

parts.note: W is the cricket abbreviation for a wide

indicators.note: in a down entry, setting a word upright means it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: to box is to spar

explanation.surface: Clothes packed in a broad box standing on its end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upright box' looks like a container standing on its end; box is the verb, meaning spar, written upwards. A wide is an extra in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Wraps are shawls or loose outer coverings worn over the shoulders, so they are items of clothing.

clue.text: Wound up line that has caught on the outside

indicators.note: being on the outside means wrapping round something, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a fish caught is netted
L is an abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A fishing line reeled in after something has snagged on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The fishing picture of a line winding up and catching is all misdirection: L goes inside NETTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Wound up is an informal way of saying irritated or annoyed, which is exactly what nettled means.

clue.text: Persistent bird tucked into decapitated mammal

indicators.note: something tucked into another thing sits inside it
decapitated means beheaded, so the first letter is cut off

parts.note: a seal is a marine mammal; without its head it becomes EAL
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A dogged seabird nestles into the body of a headless creature.
explanation.walkthrough: The decapitated mammal is the seal, a creature that a tern could plausibly sit beside, which keeps the surface coherent.
explanation.definitionFit: Persistent can mean unceasing or never-ending, which is the sense of eternal, as in eternal complaints.

clue.text: Type of property developed this decade to incorporate space

indicators.note: developed means built up or reworked, so the letters are made into something new

parts.note: taken as written
an em is a printer's space

explanation.surface: Housing built in recent years that includes some room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Developed' fits the property theme as building development, but it signals the rearrangement. EM is the printing term for a space one em wide.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-detached house shares one wall with its neighbour, a common category of British home.

clue.text: Contest featuring Oxford University is level

indicators.note: a thing featuring something includes it, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: a contest is a sporting event
OU is the abbreviation for Oxford University

explanation.surface: A competition involving Oxford ends in a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Level' reads as an adjective for a tied match, but here it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To level something is to make it flat or equal, and to even out means the same.

clue.text: Soldier possibly joins wife before heading back for port

parts.note: a soldier is one kind of ant, hence 'possibly'
W is the abbreviation for wife

indicators.note: heading back means going the opposite way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: pre- means before

explanation.surface: A serviceman meets his wife before sailing back to harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: The soldier is an insect, not a serviceman: soldier ants defend the colony.
explanation.definitionFit: Antwerp in Belgium is one of the largest seaports in Europe, so it is an example of a port.

clue.text: Up-front requirement: change old pic on Tinder

indicators.note: to change something is to alter its form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dating-app user insists the other person updates an outdated profile photo first.
explanation.walkthrough: Tinder is a dating app; the requirement to swap an old picture is the surface story, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A precondition is something that must be in place beforehand, a requirement set out in advance.

clue.text: Silicate almost cracks, showing signs of stress

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
something that cracks breaks apart, so its letters fall into a new order

parts.note: silicate without its last letter

explanation.surface: A mineral is nearly breaking apart, showing strain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stress' suggests physical strain on the mineral, but here it is emphasis in writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Slanted type is used in print to mark emphasis on words, so it signals where a reader should lay vocal weight.

clue.text: Shut your mouth after admitting lies regularly

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: since can mean after, as in 'since Tuesday'

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: first and third letters of lies

explanation.surface: Someone told to keep quiet after confessing to a string of lies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' reads as the surface's time word, but it supplies the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are blunt commands telling someone to stop talking, so the exclamation works as a direct replacement.

clue.text: Incite, say, unlimited agony

parts.note: eg, for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say'

indicators.note: without limits means without its boundaries, so the outer letters go and the middle stays

parts.note: agony without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Provoking endless suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like a verb but stands for 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: To egg someone on is to urge or encourage them to act, often rashly, which is what inciting means.

clue.text: Animal's limb badly beset by trouble

parts.note: an arm is a limb

indicators.note: to be beset is to be surrounded, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: ado means fuss or trouble
ill can mean badly, as in ill-treated

explanation.surface: A creature's leg has been hurt in some mishap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' feels like an adverb describing the injury, but it supplies a word meaning poorly; the 's after Animal is read as 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: The armadillo is an armoured American mammal, so it is a particular example of an animal.

clue.text: Significant American in pursuit of second Oscar

indicators.note: one who pursues follows behind, so the first piece comes after the others

parts.note: a second is a moment
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet
US is short for American

explanation.surface: An important US actor chasing a second Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oscar is not an award but the radio code word for O, and 'second' is a noun, not an ordinal.
explanation.definitionFit: Momentous describes an event of great importance or consequence, so it is a stronger synonym of significant.

clue.text: Leading a bike race — chortle — by 50 minutes!

parts.note: taken as written
the TT is the Isle of Man motorbike race
he-he is a chortling laugh
L is the Roman numeral for 50
M is the abbreviation for minutes

explanation.surface: A gleeful cyclist out in front by fifty minutes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading a bike race' looks like the whole definition, but only 'Leading' is; the TT (Tourist Trophy) is a famous motorcycle race on the Isle of Man.
explanation.definitionFit: Being at the helm, literally steering a ship, is an idiom for being in charge or in control.

clue.text: Hot jalapeño peppers to finish with … et voilà, Mexican food!

indicators.note: the finish is the end, so only the last letter of each word is kept

parts.note: final letters of hot, jalapeño and peppers
ta-da is the English flourish for voilà, there it is

explanation.surface: Top a dish off with spicy chillies and present it with a flourish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peppers' looks like a verb meaning sprinkles, but it is just the last of three words whose final letters are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: A tostada is a crisp fried tortilla with toppings, a dish from Mexican cooking.

clue.text: Expatiate and agree to differ about the origins of natural law

indicators.note: to differ is to become different, so the letters take a new form

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: an origin is a beginning, so the first letter of each word is used

parts.note: first letters of natural and law

explanation.surface: Two people talk at length and settle on disagreeing about where natural law began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agree to differ' is a stock phrase, but it splits: 'agree' is the material and 'to differ' the instruction. Expatiate usually takes 'on', as does enlarge.
explanation.definitionFit: To expatiate is to speak or write at length on a subject, which is the meaning of enlarge on.

clue.text: Nothing featured in new online talks is well-known

indicators.note: something featured in another thing appears within it

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
TED talks are lectures posted online
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A complaint that recent internet lectures contain nothing of note.
explanation.walkthrough: TED talks are a well-known series of short lectures published online.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means famous or celebrated, so a noted person is one who is widely recognised.

clue.text: Straight away, this place is out of contention

parts.note: now means immediately
here is this place

explanation.surface: Someone declares their present location hopeless for a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Straight away' sounds like a direction to move off, but means immediately.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitor who finishes nowhere is not placed at all, idiomatically far from winning any prize.

clue.text: Tate's opening week has Bridget Riley works in more than one section

indicators.note: an opening is a start, so only the first letter of the gallery's name is used

parts.note: first letter of Tate
W is the abbreviation for week
Bridget Riley is a leading Op Art painter

explanation.surface: The Tate gallery's launch week shows Bridget Riley paintings across several rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is a group of London art galleries; Bridget Riley is a British artist famous for optical, or Op, art.
explanation.definitionFit: Something two-part is divided into a pair of pieces, so it comes in more than a single section.

clue.text: Criminal thus called the shots and carried out scams

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked or bent, so the letters are twisted out of order

parts.note: taken as written
to call the shots is to be in charge, to lead

explanation.surface: A gang boss who gave the orders and ran confidence tricks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' reads as the noun subject of the sentence, but it is an adjective telling you to mix up the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: To hustle is to swindle or con people, so someone who hustled ran fraudulent schemes.

clue.text: Very skilled person made money to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent means partly, so only part of the phrase is used

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: An expert who earned a modest amount.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made money' seems to be the person's achievement, but the letters sit across the join of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A demon can mean someone remarkably good or energetic at an activity, as in a demon bowler.

clue.text: Endlessly travelled around, having left part of Wales

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
endless means without an end, so the final letter is removed

parts.note: went means travelled; without its tail it is WEN
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Someone has wandered aimlessly before departing from a Welsh region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the past tense of leave, but it is the nautical left side.
explanation.definitionFit: Newport is a city in south-east Wales, so it is one particular place within that country.

clue.text: Plan 24 hours in Ibiza? Good stuff!

parts.note: dia is Spanish for day, as spoken on the Spanish island of Ibiza
G is the abbreviation for good
to stuff is to ram or cram

explanation.surface: Organising a day of partying on Ibiza sounds like a great idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good stuff!' reads as an exclamation of approval, but splits into G and a verb meaning cram.
explanation.definitionFit: A diagram is a drawn plan or schematic showing how something is laid out.

clue.text: Cookie containing odd bits of grain and herb

indicators.note: to contain is to hold within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the Oreo is a well-known sandwich biscuit

indicators.note: the odd-numbered positions, first, third and fifth, are the ones kept

parts.note: letters one, three and five of grain

explanation.surface: A biscuit with a few cereal grains and some herb mixed in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd bits' sounds like random crumbs, but it means the odd-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregano is an aromatic plant used in cooking, so it is one example of a culinary herb.

clue.text: Unite extremists to do what's necessary financially

definitions.meaning: first meaning, taken literally: bring people at the far ends together
second meaning: earn just enough to cover one's costs

explanation.surface: Bringing radicals together to balance the books.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a playful literal reading: extremists are people at the ends, so uniting them means bringing ends together.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means having just enough income to pay for one's living costs, getting by financially.
